name: Non-Decreasing Dilemma
description: Alice has recently received an array $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ for her birthday! She is very proud of her array, and when she showed her friend Bob the array, he was very happy with her present too! However, soon Bob became curious, and as any sane friend would do, asked Alice to perform $$$q$$$ operations of two types on her array: $$$1$$$ $$$x$$$ $$$y$$$: update the element $$$a_x$$$ to $$$y$$$ (set $$$a_x = y$$$). $$$2$$$ $$$l$$$ $$$r$$$: calculate how many non-decreasing subarrays exist within the subarray $$$[a_l, a_{l+1}, \dots, a_r]$$$. More formally, count the number of pairs of integers $$$(p,q)$$$ such that $$$l \le p \le q \le r$$$ and $$$a_p \le a_{p+1} \le \dots \le a_{q-1} \le a_q$$$. Help Alice answer Bob's queries!
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le n, q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the size of the array, and the number of queries, respectively. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the elements of Alice's array. The next $$$q$$$ lines consist of three integers each. The first integer of the $$$i$$$-th line is $$$t_i$$$, the operation being performed on the $$$i$$$-th step ($$$t_i = 1$$$ or $$$t_i = 2$$$). If $$$t_i = 1$$$, the next two integers are $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i \le n$$$; $$$1 \le y_i \le 10^9$$$), updating the element at position $$$x_i$$$ to $$$y_i$$$ (setting $$$a_{x_i} = y_i$$$). If $$$t_i = 2$$$, the next two integers are $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le n$$$), the two indices Bob asks Alice about for the $$$i$$$-th query. It's guaranteed that there is at least one operation of the second type.
output_specification: For each query of type $$$2$$$, print a single integer, the answer to the query.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1567E — Non-Decreasing Dilemma [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
